question: Recent discussions at EU level, including in the Committee on Petitions (PETI), have highlighted regulatory gaps regarding noise emissions from wind farms and their potential impact on public health and quality of life. The Commission has acknowledged that noise from wind farms is not specifically regulated in EU legislation and that existing methodologies do not fully capture low-frequency noise and infrasound. In this context: 1.

Does the Commission intend to propose specific EU rules or guidelines on noise from wind farms, including harmonised methods for measuring, monitoring and assessing low-frequency noise and infrasound?
How will the Commission ensure that when EU noise policy is updated in future it will take due account of technological developments and the cumulative effects of wind farms on nearby residents?

Will the Commission consider introducing minimum protection standards for affected residents, such as mandatory acoustic studies, enhanced health impact assessments or guidelines for the precautionary siting of new projects?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) As stated in the reply to written question E-000019/2026, the Environmental Noise Directive (END)1 remains the main EU legislative instrument for addressing excessive noise pollution. The END is focused on traffic noise and noise from the industrial activities listed in Annex I of the Industrial Emissions Directive (IED)2.

However, the IED does not cover the generation of electricity from wind turbines. Windfarm projects can nonetheless be subject to an Environmental Impact Assessment3. In that case noise emissions must be assessed and measures identified to address possible adverse effects.

In 2018, the World Health Organization (WHO) developed guidelines4 to provide recommendations for protecting human health from exposure to environmental noise originating from various sources, including wind turbines.

While the WHO conditionally recommended keeping audible wind turbine noise below 45 decibel day–evening–night noise level to prevent annoyance and sleep disturbance, due to the lack of sufficient scientific evidence, it did not propose specific limits or guidelines regarding infrasound.

At the current stage of scientific and policy development on noise at global and EU level, it therefore remains the primary responsibility of the Member States to secure the protection of citizens affected by the noise produced by wind turbines, by defining and enforcing, where appropriate and taking into account the local circumstances, specific noise requirements which may use the thresholds recommended by the WHO.
1 Directive 2002/49/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 June 2002 relating to the

assessment and management of environmental noise, OJ L 189 18.7.2002, p. 12. 2 Directive (EU) 2024/1785 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 April 2024 amending Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council on industrial emissions (integrated pollution Prevention and control) and Council Directive 1999/31/EC on the landfill of waste, OJ L, 2024/1785, 15.7.2024.

3 In accordance with Directive 2011/92/EU as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU. Directive 2014/52/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 amending Directive 2011/92/EU on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 124, 25.4.2014. 4 https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789289053563.
